title: Column stores and compression
goal: By the end, you can explain why storing a table by column lets a report read a small part of the bytes, squeeze a column with dictionary, run-length and bit-packing encodings, use each chunk's smallest and largest value to skip it unread, and build a compressed column chunk that does both.
opening:
Picture a café owner at the end of the month with a shoebox of paper receipts, one for every card payment. Each receipt shows the date and time, the card, what was bought, the currency and the amount. She wants one number, the month's takings. So she picks up every receipt, reads past everything else on it, and adds up the amounts.

A database does the same, and that surprises people. `SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM payments` names one column, so it feels as if only that column gets read. In PostgreSQL, a free database program, it reads the whole table: 66 MB to add up 8 MB of amounts.

In Query optimization and cardinality estimates, the planner chose how to read each table, but every plan it chose still read whole rows. In this lesson, we'll store a table by column instead, squeeze each column to a fraction of its size, and skip most of it without reading it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A `payments` table in PostgreSQL has six columns and 1,000,000 rows, and takes about 66 MB on disk. One column, `amount_cents`, holds each amount as an 8-byte number. Roughly how much of the table does `SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM payments` read?
options: About 8 MB: one 8-byte number per row
All of it, about 66 MB: every part of the table holds some amounts
About 33 MB: half the table, on average
Almost nothing: PostgreSQL keeps a running total for each column
warmup.why: PostgreSQL stores whole rows together, so every page of the table (an 8 KB block) holds some amounts, and the scan must read every page: 8,404 pages, 66 MB, in the first Try it. Reading only 8 MB needs the amounts stored next to each other, which is what a column store does. And PostgreSQL keeps no running totals. Its statistics, the summary of each column it uses for planning, hold samples and counts, not sums.

sections.h: Adding up one column means reading all six
sections.body:
A small company runs the program that records card payments for cafés, bookshops and grocers, and keeps its data in PostgreSQL. A database keeps data in tables, like the sheets of a spreadsheet: each row is one record, and each column holds one piece of it. In the Try it, the `payments` table has 1,000,000 rows and six columns. They hold an id, the shop that was paid (`merchant_id`: the labs call a shop a merchant), the currency, a status, the amount in cents and the time. At the end of the month, someone asks for the total in SQL, the language most databases understand: `SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM payments`. A question written in SQL is called a query.

The query needs 8 bytes from each row, the amount. To answer it, PostgreSQL scans the table, reading it from start to end: all 8,404 pages, 66 MB. (A page is the 8 KB block a database reads from disk at a time.) The query uses one column, and the scan pays for six.

That follows from how PostgreSQL stores a table. Its heap, the file of a table's rows from Pages, tuples and heap files (lesson 2 of this track), fills each page with whole rows, one after another. Each row is a 24-byte header, PostgreSQL's own notes about the row, followed by its six values: 64 bytes in all here. So every page holds some amounts, and the scan reads every page, though most of each page is ids, shops, currencies, statuses and times. Keeping complete rows together is called the row layout, or the N-ary storage model (NSM), and a database that stores tables this way is a row store.

The shoebox from the opening is a row store, one receipt per payment with every detail on it.

For the work the app does all day, the row layout is right. Recording a payment writes one row into one page. Fetching payment 42 by its id reads one page and gets every column at once. A report is the opposite case: a few columns of millions of rows. That's analytics: questions about many rows at once. The monthly report adds up amounts by currency over 50 million payments, and needs two columns out of six.

A second layout turns the table on its side. It keeps each column in its own array, a list of values one after another, in row order. Row 1 is the first value of every array, row 2 the second, so the database can put any row back together from its position. `sum(amount_cents)` now reads one array of 1,000,000 x 8 bytes = 8 MB instead of 66 MB, before any compression (squeezing the data smaller). That's the **column layout**, also called the decomposition storage model (DSM), and a database that stores tables this way is a column store.

In the shoebox, that means cutting every receipt into strips, one strip per detail, and keeping one binder per detail, with the strips in the same order. To total the amounts, you open one binder.

It has a price. Recording one payment writes to six arrays, and fetching one whole payment reads from six places: six binders, opened at the same position. Column stores accept that, because their users load data in big batches and read it with big scans. They also don't keep a column as one endless array. They cut the table into row groups, slices of so many rows, and store each column of a row group separately. DuckDB, a free analytics database that runs inside your own program, uses row groups of 122,880 rows. Parquet, a common file format for tables stored by column, is a series of row groups, each with one column chunk per column. A scan of one column reads one chunk per row group. Chunks are what the next two sections squeeze and skip, starting with the squeezing.

try.title: Count the pages a one-column sum reads
steps: From the `labs` folder, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`. Docker runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, so nothing gets installed on your computer. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's command window where you type SQL: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.
Paste the statements below. They create `payments` with six columns and 1,000,000 made-up rows; the first one drops the table if an earlier lesson left one. The next Try its use it too.

Read the table's size, the average size of a row and the size of the amount. Predict how many pages `sum(amount_cents)` touches. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` runs the query and shows its steps, and `Buffers` counts the pages each step touched. Check your guess there.

refs.title: Parquet: file format (row groups and column chunks)

sections.h: One column's values look alike, so they squeeze small
sections.body:
Put a column's values next to each other, and they turn out to be very repetitive. The `currency` column of a million payments holds four different strings, or pieces of text. `status` holds three. `amount_cents` holds numbers below 100,000, each in an 8-byte slot that could hold numbers up to about 9 quintillion (a 9 with 18 zeros after it). `created_at` rises by 2 seconds from one row to the next.

A first idea is to run a general-purpose compressor over each column: a program such as gzip or zstd that shrinks any file, the way you zip files before you email them. But every scan pays to unzip everything it touches, and reading one value means unzipping the block around it. DuckDB's engineers explained in 2022 why their tables mostly avoid such compressors. They're slow to undo, they need blocks of about 256 KB to work well, and they hide the shape of the data from the rest of the database.

A second idea uses **lightweight encodings**. Each one is built for one pattern in the data, and is cheap enough to undo in the middle of a scan. They count in bits: a bit is a single 0 or 1, and 8 bits make a byte. A number from 0 to 3 fits in 2 bits, and a number up to 16,383 in 14.

- Dictionary encoding stores each distinct value once, in a sorted list, and replaces every value by its position in the list, a small number called a code. Four currencies become codes 0 to 3. Because the list is sorted, `currency < 'GBP'` can be tested on the codes.
- Bit-packing stores each number in the fewest bits that hold the largest one. Codes 0 to 3 need 2 bits, so a million currencies take 250 KB. With a frame of reference, the chunk's smallest value is subtracted first. Then amounts from 0 to 99,999 need 17 bits instead of 64, and the times of one hour need 12 bits once the hour's first second is subtracted.
- Run-length encoding (RLE) stores a value once, with the number of times it repeats in a row. It wins on sorted or slowly changing columns: a `status` column sorted by status is three runs, however many rows the table has.

Here the binders stop being a good picture. A binder of paper strips that all say EUR is as thick as one with mixed currencies. A column chunk of a thousand EURs becomes one dictionary entry and one run.

The encodings stack: dictionary codes are then bit-packed or run-length encoded, as the stepper shows. And none of them wins everywhere. A chunk of random 64-bit numbers gains nothing from any of them, and RLE on data without runs makes it bigger. So engines decide chunk by chunk. DuckDB looks at each segment of a column (its word for a chunk), tries its encodings and keeps the smallest. In the Try it, it chose bit-packing for the four number columns and DICT_FSST for the two text columns. That's a dictionary whose strings are squeezed again with FSST, a method that replaces common pieces of text with one-byte codes. The whole table takes 5.5 MB on disk, against PostgreSQL's 66 MB heap. Your lab's `ColumnChunk.of` makes the same choice between three encodings.

Next, we'll skip chunks without reading them at all.

aside.title: Disks are cheap. Why squeeze the data at all?
aside.body: Space is the smaller win. A scan spends most of its time moving bytes: from the disk into memory, and from memory into the processor. A currency column of 250 KB instead of 7 MB moves about 28 times fewer bytes, and it stays in memory more easily. Undoing a 2-bit code costs the processor a few simple steps, far less than waiting for the bytes it replaced.

sections.h: Writing down each chunk's smallest and largest value, so a scan can skip it
sections.body:
Squeezing makes each chunk smaller. But a query about one day, with the condition `WHERE created_at` on October 15, still decodes every chunk of `created_at`: it turns the codes back into values to find the matching rows. (`WHERE` keeps only the rows that pass a test.) The fix costs almost nothing. When the engine writes a chunk, it also notes the chunk's smallest and largest value. That pair is a **zone map**, also called a min-max index. In the binders, it's the first and last date written on the spine of each date binder.

Before decoding a chunk, the scan compares the chunk's range, from its min to its max, with the condition. If the day lies outside it, no row in the chunk can match, and the chunk is skipped unread. If the whole chunk lies inside the condition, every row matches, and `count(*)`, which counts rows, can add the chunk's row count without decoding it either. Otherwise the chunk is decoded and its rows checked one by one, as the stepper shows.

In the DuckDB demo, each row group of 122,880 payments covers about 2.8 days, and a one-day query scans 2 of the 9 row groups, the two that overlap October 15. DuckDB keeps a zone map for every column of every row group without being asked.

Zone maps only work when a column's values follow the order of the rows on disk. Payments arrive in time order, so `created_at` and `id` rise from chunk to chunk, and each chunk covers a narrow slice. `amount_cents` is in random order. Every chunk holds amounts from almost 0 to almost 100,000, so every zone map overlaps every range, and nothing is skipped. The demo shuffles the same rows into a second table, and the one-day query then scans 9 row groups of 9.

**A zone map can only skip what the load order kept together. Load the data sorted by the column you filter on.**

PostgreSQL has zone maps too, as a kind of index, an extra structure that helps find rows without reading the whole table. A **BRIN** index (block range index) stores the min and max of a column for every 128 pages, by default. On the 1,000,000 payments in time order, it takes 24 kB. A B+tree index on the same column takes 21 MB: that's the usual kind of index, from B+trees (lesson 4 of this track), which points to every row. The one-day query through the BRIN index reads 512 of the 8,404 pages and rechecks the rows in them. On the shuffled copy, the same kind of index reads all 8,384 pages. BRIN fits tables that only ever grow at the end and are asked about by time, such as a log of every change to the accounts. A B+tree finds rows more exactly and works in any order, at about 900 times the size.

Cloud services keep zone maps for every file they write. Next, we'll see what that does to a query's cost.

sections.h: The same trick at cloud scale: Snowflake and Redshift
sections.body:
Big companies keep their analytics data in a data warehouse, a column store that holds years of a company's records for reports. Snowflake, Redshift (from Amazon) and BigQuery (from Google) are three that companies rent as cloud services. Their data lives in object storage, a cloud service that keeps files cheaply, and the last two sections decide most of what a query costs there.

Snowflake cuts every table into **micro-partitions** of 50 to 500 MB of data before compression, stored compressed, each column separately. For every micro-partition, it keeps notes outside the data: each column's range of values and its number of distinct values. A query's WHERE condition is checked against those notes first, and a micro-partition that can't match is never fetched. That skipping is called pruning. Snowflake's own example of the ideal case: a year of hourly data, queried for one hour, reads 1/8,760 of the micro-partitions.

Ideal is the catch, and it's the shuffled table from the last section again. Snowflake fills micro-partitions in the order rows are inserted or loaded. Payments loaded in time order prune well by date. A condition on the shop mostly doesn't, because every micro-partition holds hundreds of shops, and its range for `merchant_id` covers nearly all of them. Snowflake measures this as clustering depth: for a column, the average number of micro-partitions whose ranges overlap. It's at least 1 for a table with data, and lower is better. Declare a clustering key, the columns to keep the data sorted by, and Snowflake sorts the data again in the background to keep the depth down, and bills you for the computing time. Updates and deletes scatter new rows around, so the depth drifts back up.

Amazon Redshift does the same with smaller pieces and more control. It stores each column in 1 MB blocks and keeps every block's min and max, its zone maps. You choose a sort key when you create a table (or let `SORTKEY AUTO` choose it), and rows are stored in that order. A range condition on the sort key skips blocks: AWS's example is five years of data sorted by date, where a one-month query skips up to 98% of the blocks. A compound sort key works like an index on several columns from Indexes and reading EXPLAIN (lesson 7 of this track): it helps conditions on its first column, or its first few. An interleaved sort key gives each column equal weight, and costs more to keep sorted.

Writes are the weak spot. Changing one value inside a sorted, compressed file means writing a new file. So warehouses collect new rows and write them out in bulk as new files, the pattern of LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters (lesson 5 of this track) again. Some changes need no rewrite at all: in Snowflake, deleting every row of a table only changes the notes.

The open version of this design is Parquet files in object storage, with a min and max for every column chunk. DuckDB reads them, and so do Spark and Trino, programs that spread one big query over many computers. Next, we'll put all the pieces together, and see what a column store is bad at.

try.title: Predict what a warehouse skips
steps: No Docker here: work it out on paper, then check the answer. A Snowflake table holds two years of card payments in 2,000 micro-partitions, loaded in time order, so each micro-partition covers about 9 hours.

For each query, guess how many micro-partitions are read: (a) `WHERE created_at` on one day; (b) `WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042'`, a shop that takes payments every day; (c) `WHERE currency = 'SEK'`, 5% of payments, spread evenly; (d) the same as (b), after adding the clustering key `(merchant_id, created_at)` and letting Snowflake sort the data again, for a table of 10,000 shops.
Then say which of the four you'd expect to get slower over a year of updates to old payments, and why.
try.expect: (a) About 3 or 4. Two years is about 17,500 hours in 2,000 micro-partitions, so each covers about 9 hours, and one day overlaps 3 or 4 of them. The ranges on `created_at` are narrow because the load order is time order. (b) Almost all 2,000. The shop takes payments every day, so its id falls inside nearly every micro-partition's range for `merchant_id`. A range can only rule out a micro-partition when it misses the value. (c) Almost all 2,000. SEK is in every micro-partition, and a dictionary or a distinct count doesn't change that. A column store still wins here, by reading one or two columns of each micro-partition instead of all of them. (d) A handful. Sorted by shop first, each micro-partition holds a few of the 10,000 shops (about 5 each), so M-0042's rows sit in one or two of them, and their `merchant_id` ranges rule out the rest. The clustered table is the one that gets slower. Updates write rows into new micro-partitions in the order they arrive, the ranges start to overlap again, and the clustering depth rises. Snowflake's background sorting, billed as computing time, works to bring it back down. (a) stays good as long as loads stay in time order.

sections.h: What column stores are bad at, and where each layout belongs
sections.body:
Put the pieces together. An analytics scan in a column store touches only the columns the query names, reads them compressed, and skips chunks by their zone maps. It hands the rest to a vectorized executor, the part that runs the query, of the kind from Query execution: iterators, joins and vectors (lesson 9 of this track). It works through a batch of values from one column in one tight loop. DuckDB's batches, which it calls vectors, hold 2,048 values. Some engines go further and filter the compressed data directly. A condition on `currency` becomes a comparison of 2-bit codes, and only the row positions that pass are used to fetch values from the other columns. That's called late materialization: rows are put back together as late as possible.

The same design makes single-row work expensive. Changing one payment's status means finding the value inside a compressed chunk, and rewriting a whole chunk for one value is wasteful. So column stores usually record changes on the side, for example as a list of deleted row positions, and rewrite chunks later. And reading one whole payment reads one chunk from each of six columns, against one page in a heap.

That's where people go wrong with a column store. They feed it the way they'd feed PostgreSQL: one insert per payment as it happens, or an update every time a status changes. Many column stores write each small insert as its own little file, with its own zone map, and then spend their time merging what one batch would have written once. The code for one insert looks just like the code for a batch, so it's an easy trap. **A column store wants big batches. Collect rows and load thousands at a time.** Record a status change as a new row instead of an update, and sort each batch by the column you filter on most.

So the two layouts end up in different places in a payments company. The records the app handles one at a time, such as each payment as it happens and each account's balance, stay in a row store such as PostgreSQL. There, each request touches a few rows by key. Reports, fraud studies and checks that the company's totals match the bank's run on a column store. That can be DuckDB inside a program, a warehouse such as Snowflake, Redshift or BigQuery, or Parquet files in object storage. Data moves from one side to the other in batches, through a nightly export or a feed that copies every change as it happens. PostgreSQL itself stays a row store by default, though add-ons (extensions) can give it tables stored by column.

Even a column store still adds up all 50 million amounts each time someone asks for the monthly total. The next lesson keeps the answer instead.

worked.title: Bit-pack eight currency codes by hand

steps.say: Eight payments' currencies. Build the sorted dictionary, and replace each value by its code, its position in the list.
steps.code:
values:     EUR EUR GBP EUR USD EUR SEK EUR
dictionary: 0 = EUR, 1 = GBP, 2 = SEK, 3 = USD
codes:      0   0   1   0   3   0   2   0

steps.say: The largest code is 3, so each code needs `bitsFor(3)` = 2 bits. Value `i` goes into bits `2i` and `2i + 1` of one 64-bit word, a `Long`. (`numberOfLeadingZeros` counts the zero bits in front of the first 1.)
Put each code in place: shift it left to its position (`shl`) and combine it with the word (`or`, which keeps every bit that's set in either). Only three codes aren't zero.
steps.code:
word = (1 shl 4) or (3 shl 8) or (2 shl 12)
     = 16 + 768 + 8192 = 8976
     = 0b10_00_11_00_01_00_00   (pairs from value 6 down to value 0)

steps.say: Read value 4 back: shift the word right by 8 bits (`ushr`) and keep the lowest 2 bits (`and 0b11`). Then look the code up in the dictionary.

With wider values, a code can be split across two words. The lab's `decode` takes the low part from one word and the high part from the next. For 17-bit amounts, value 3 starts at bit 51, and its top 4 bits are in word 1.
steps.code:
val pos = i.toLong() * bits                 // 3 * 17 = 51
val word = (pos / 64).toInt()               // 0
val offset = (pos % 64).toInt()             // 51
var x = words[word] ushr offset             // 13 low bits
if (offset + bits > 64) x = x or (words[word + 1] shl (64 - offset))  // 4 high bits
val value = base + (x and ((1L shl bits) - 1))

steps.say: Count the bytes. Plain, the eight strings take 8 x (4 + 3) = 56 bytes. Encoded, they take the dictionary (4 x 7 = 28 bytes) plus 16 bits of codes. The dictionary is paid once per chunk, so on a chunk of 2,048 values the codes cost 512 bytes against 14,336.
steps.code:
plain:   8 x 7            = 56 bytes
encoded: 28 + 2           = 30 bytes
2,048 values: 28 + 512    = 540 bytes, against 14,336

lab.title: Build a compressed column chunk with zone maps
steps: Read the top of `Encodings.kt`: the `Encoded` interface, `Plain`, `bitsFor()` and the size formula of each encoding. Then run the tests once with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code, and all 11 fail for now.
Write `RunLength.encode()` and `RunLength.decode()`. The two run-length tests pass, including one where a sorted status column gets 13,000 times smaller.

Write `BitPacked.encode()` and `BitPacked.decode()`, frame of reference included. The round-trip test encodes values and checks that decoding gives them back, for every width from 1 to 64 bits, so it covers values that are split across two words.
Write `Dictionary.encode()`, then `ColumnChunk.of()` in `Column.kt`. It keeps the smallest of the three encodings and records the chunk's min and max.
Write `Column.countBetween()`: for each chunk, skip it, count it whole or decode it, as its zone map allows. Run the tests until all 11 pass.
hints: In `BitPacked.encode`, compute positions with Longs: `val pos = i.toLong() * bits`. The word is `pos / 64` and the offset `pos % 64`. The part that spills into the next word exists only when `offset + bits > 64`, and it's `x ushr (64 - offset)`.
`values.max() - base` is right even when the range needs all 64 bits: the subtraction wraps around, and `bitsFor` reads the result as unsigned. Decoding adds `base` back with the same wrap.
For the mask in `decode`, `(1L shl bits) - 1` fails at 64 bits, because a shift by 64 is a shift by 0 on the JVM. Use `-1L` when `bits == 64`.
In `countBetween`, test the skip case first (`max < lo || min > hi`), then the whole-chunk case (`lo <= min && max <= hi`). Increase `chunksDecoded` only when you call `decode()`.

recap: A row store keeps whole rows together, so a scan of one column reads every page: 66 MB to add up 8 MB of amounts in the Try it. A column store keeps each column's values together, in row order, and rebuilds a row from its position.
Column stores cut tables into row groups (122,880 rows in DuckDB; a Parquet file is a series of row groups) and store each column of a row group as its own chunk.

Dictionary encoding swaps values for small codes into a sorted list. Bit-packing stores numbers in the fewest bits, after subtracting the chunk's smallest value (frame of reference). Run-length encoding stores a run of equal values once. Engines try several per chunk and keep the smallest: DuckDB stored the 1,000,000 payments in 5.5 MB, against PostgreSQL's 66 MB.

A zone map is a chunk's min and max. A scan skips chunks whose range misses the condition and counts chunks that lie inside it, but only when the column follows the order of the rows on disk. PostgreSQL's BRIN index is a zone map for every 128 pages.

Cloud warehouses skip data the same way at a larger scale: Snowflake keeps value ranges for every 50 to 500 MB micro-partition, and Redshift a min and max for every 1 MB block. The load order, clustering keys and sort keys decide how much a query reads.

The limit: column stores are slow at single-row work. Changing or fetching one payment touches a chunk of every column, and rows added one at a time squeeze badly, so data is copied into them in batches.
closing:
We started with a shoebox of receipts, and an owner reading every one to add up the amounts. With one binder per detail, the amounts sit together and squeeze to a fraction of their size. Each binder carries its first and last value on the spine, so most stay shut.

If you ever meet a Parquet file, DuckDB's command-line program shows its zone maps: `SELECT row_group_id, path_in_schema, stats_min, stats_max FROM parquet_metadata('file.parquet');` lists the min and max of every column chunk.

Next, we'll stop adding up 50 million amounts every time someone asks for the monthly total, and find out how a database can keep the answer, and keep it right.

quiz.q: A table of 10 million payments is sorted by `status`, which has three values. Which encoding stores the `status` column, chunk by chunk, in the fewest bytes?
options: A dictionary with bit-packed codes: 2 bits per row
Run-length encoding of the dictionary codes: one run per status per chunk
The plain strings, squeezed with gzip
Bit-packing the bytes of the strings
quiz.why: Sorted by status, almost every chunk holds one status, so it's a single run: a value and a count, however long the chunk is. Bit-packed codes still cost 2 bits per row, 2.5 MB for 10 million rows. Gzip would squeeze it well too, but every scan would pay to unzip it, which is why column stores prefer lightweight encodings.

quiz.q: A chunk holds 2,048 amounts between 1,000 and 66,535 cents. With a frame of reference and bit-packing, how many bits does each value take?
options: 17, because the largest value is above 65,535
16, because 66,535 - 1,000 = 65,535 fits in 16 bits
64, as a Long
8, because most payments are small
quiz.why: A frame of reference subtracts the chunk's smallest value first, so the numbers to store run from 0 to 65,535, which is exactly 16 bits. Without the subtraction, 66,535 needs 17 bits. Bit-packing uses one width for the whole chunk, set by its largest value, so many small payments don't lower it.

quiz.q: Payments are loaded in time order into a column store with zone maps. Which query can skip most chunks?
options: `WHERE amount_cents > 99000`
`WHERE merchant_id = 42`
`WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-15' AND created_at < '2026-10-16'`
`WHERE currency = 'SEK'`
quiz.why: Only `created_at` follows the load order, so each chunk covers a narrow slice of time, and most zone maps rule out a one-day range. Amounts, shops and currencies are mixed in every chunk, so every chunk's min and max take in the value asked for, and nothing is skipped. Sorting the data by shop would let the shop query skip instead.

quiz.q: Which job belongs in a row store rather than a column store?
options: Adding up amounts by currency over 50 million payments
Fetching one payment with all its columns by its id, 5,000 times a second
Counting payments per day for a year
Reading a month of payments to check them against the bank's statement
quiz.why: Fetching a whole row by its id reads one page in a row store, and one chunk per column, often compressed, in a column store. The other three read a few columns of many rows, which is exactly what a column store is built for.

quiz.q: From Pages, tuples and heap files: a heap row has a 24-byte header, and each row also needs a 4-byte pointer at the top of its page. In the first Try it, each `payments` row takes 64 bytes, and 119 rows fit in an 8 KB page. About what share of the bytes a `sum(amount_cents)` scan reads are amounts?
options: About 12%
About 50%
About 100%
About 25%
quiz.why: 119 rows x 8 bytes = 952 bytes of amounts in an 8,192-byte page, about 12%. The rest is headers, pointers and the other five columns, all read because a heap page stores whole rows. A column store reads only the 8-byte amounts, and fewer bytes still once they're bit-packed.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between the row layout (NSM) and the column layout (DSM)?
flashcards.back: NSM stores whole rows together. DSM stores each column's values together, and rebuilds a row from its position.
Each distinct value once, in a sorted list, and for each row a small number: the value's position in the list.

flashcards.front: What is a frame of reference?
flashcards.back: Subtracting the chunk's smallest value from every value before bit-packing, so the numbers need fewer bits.
When equal values sit in long runs, as in sorted or slowly changing columns. On data without runs, it makes the chunk bigger.
A chunk's min and max, kept outside it, so a scan can skip the chunk, or count it whole, without decoding it.

flashcards.front: When do zone maps skip nothing?
flashcards.back: When the column's values don't follow the order of the rows on disk: then every chunk's range covers almost all values.

flashcards.front: What do Snowflake micro-partitions and Redshift blocks keep, and when does it help?
flashcards.back: Snowflake: each column's range of values and number of distinct values, for every 50 to 500 MB micro-partition. Redshift: a min and max for every 1 MB block. It skips data only when the table is clustered or sorted on the column you filter on.

terms.plain: Storing whole rows one after another, as PostgreSQL's heap does.
Storing each column's values together, in row order.
A slice of a table, such as 122,880 rows in DuckDB, whose columns are stored as separate chunks.
Replacing values by small codes that point into a list of the distinct values.
Storing each number in the fewest bits that hold the largest one in its chunk.
Storing a run of equal values once, with its length.
A chunk's min and max, kept so a scan can skip chunks that can't match.
PostgreSQL's block range index: a min and max for each group of pages.

explain_back.prompt: Your team copies 50 million payments a month into Parquet files for its reports. Explain to a friend why a query for one day's EUR payments reads so little of the files, and what you'd change if it read everything.
explain_back.answer: Parquet stores the rows in row groups, and inside each row group every column is a separate chunk. The query reads only the columns it names, so the other columns cost nothing. Each chunk is encoded: the currency as a small dictionary with codes of a few bits, the amounts bit-packed after subtracting the chunk's smallest value, and the times the same way. So the bytes it reads are a small part of the raw size. Each column chunk also records its min and max. If the file was written in time order, most row groups cover other days, their min and max rule out the day asked for, and the reader skips them without reading their data. If the query reads everything, the likely cause is that the rows aren't in date order, so every row group spans the whole month and no zone map can rule anything out. I'd sort the export by payment date (and maybe by currency) before writing it, and keep the row groups big enough that each chunk squeezes well.

deeper.body:
**PAX and row groups.** Anastassia Ailamaki and colleagues proposed PAX (Partition Attributes Across) in 2001: one block still holds whole rows, but inside the block the values are grouped by column. Row groups in Parquet and DuckDB are the same idea at a larger scale. A row is never spread across files, yet a scan reads only the columns it needs.

**More encodings.** Delta encoding stores the difference from the previous value, which suits times and ids that only go up. Numbers with fractions, called floating-point numbers, need their own methods; DuckDB has used Chimp, Patas and ALP for them. FSST squeezes strings by replacing common pieces of up to 8 bytes with one-byte codes, and keeps each string readable on its own. Parquet's own encodings include a dictionary, a mix of run-length and bit-packing, and delta encodings, with an optional general-purpose compressor such as zstd on top.

**Scanning compressed data in batches.** Bit-packed and dictionary-coded chunks are arrays of small numbers. So a filter can compare codes with SIMD instructions, processor instructions that work on several values at once, and produce a selection vector, the list of positions that matched. It's the same structure the batch filter in Query execution: iterators, joins and vectors builds.

**BigQuery.** Google's warehouse stores tables in Capacitor, a column format that grew out of the ideas in Google's Dremel paper for nested and repeated fields. You control how much it skips with partitioning and clustering columns, the same trade as a Snowflake clustering key.

**Newer file formats.** Andy Pavlo's review of 2025 lists several new open column formats (FastLanes, Vortex and F3 among them) built to decode faster on modern hardware. It also notes that most Parquet files in use still rely only on features from 2013.
